entities.summary:
Ye Shi (1150–1223), courtesy name Zhengze (正则) and pseudonym Mr. Shuixin (水心先生), was a preeminent Chinese neo-Confucian scholar, official, and intellectual leader of the Southern Song dynasty. Hailing from Wenzhou, Zhejiang, he became a pivotal figure of the Yongjia School, a distinctive intellectual current known for its emphasis on practical statecraft, economic prosperity, and robust military defense. Unlike the more introspective and metaphysical strands of neo-Confucianism championed by contemporaries like Zhu Xi, Ye Shi advocated for a Confucianism deeply engaged with the concrete realities of governance, believing that moral cultivation must manifest in effective administration and a strong nation. His profound commitment to the "utility of the world" (經世致用, jingshi zhiyong) marked him as a pragmatic idealist in a period of intense intellectual and political ferment.

Throughout his distinguished bureaucratic career, Ye Shi served in various capacities, including as a prefect and censor, continually advocating for policies rooted in his practical philosophy. He vehemently criticized the prevailing tendency towards abstract speculation and quietistic meditation, arguing that such approaches detached scholars from their duty to serve the state and its people. His extensive writings, including the "Shuixin Wenji" (Collected Works of Shuixin), articulate a comprehensive vision for national strength, emphasizing agricultural development, sound financial management, and a proactive military posture against northern invaders. He famously debated against the intellectual paradigms of both Zhu Xi and Lu Jiuyuan, asserting that true knowledge was inseparable from action and that moral principles found their ultimate validation in effective governance and societal well-being.
